stories.title: Pakistan's Munir spoke to Trump ahead of Tehran visit, sources say
stories.summary: Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir spoke with U.S. President Donald Trump last week, according to three Pakistani sources, days before Munir was expected to hold talks in the Iranian capital Tehran on Monday. The call, which has not been previously reported, came as the U.S. threatened to roll out major economic sanctions targeting Iran and its trade partners. The White House Office of the Press Secretary did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It was unclear what Munir and Trump discussed. Pakistan's military confirmed the visit on Monday, saying it was "part of Pakistan’s efforts to promote regional peace and stability." Iranian officials had confirmed the visit on Sunday, saying it was focused on security and peace. Trump last week warned of economic consequences against any country that provided "any type of lifeline to Iran" as he seeks to isolate the Islamic Republic. Iran in turn vowed to shut down all oil exports from the Gulf. Pakistan, which has played a key mediating role between the U.S. and Iran this year, has remained a trading partner of Iran throughout the recent fighting. Munir was expected to meet with people close to Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Monday, one Pakistani source said. Another Pakistani government source said while U.S.-Iran tensions were a focus of the visit, Munir was also expected to discuss recent attacks by Iran-aligned Houthi fighters on Pakistan's ally Saudi Arabia as well as the recently signed mutual defence agreement between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Pakistan's earlier mediation efforts between the U.S. and Iran resulted in an interim peace agreement signed in June. But the Islamabad Memorandum quickly faltered, amid new fighting between Iran and the U.S. that has threatened to spiral into a wider regional conflict in recent weeks.

stories.title: UK's rarest bird of prey rears new chicks in secret location
stories.summary: The UK's rarest bird of prey has successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) has reported. A male Montagu's harrier, known as "AU" by conservationists, bred with two different females, rearing six chicks across two nests on English farmland. Montagu's harriers were put on a "red list" of birds most at risk in the UK in 2021. Numbers have declined from a high of nine successful nests in 2011, to no evidence of successful breeding between 2020 and 2024. An RSPB spokesperson said: "We are doing our absolute utmost to save this iconic species in the UK and are delighted with six flying juveniles this year." Four chicks hatched in the same secret location last year. The charity said careful monitoring, in partnership with the farmers on whose land the birds nested, meant the nests were protected by fences to exclude ground predators such as foxes. The single male Montagu's harrier has also been working very hard to keep his two nests of hungry chicks fed. The BBC was given exclusive access to the nest and was able to witness some of the spectacular feeding behaviour of the raptors: the male drops prey in mid-air and the female rolls upside down to catch it in her talons. These slender, long-winged raptors make an epic annual migration to Africa in winter and return to Europe to nest over summer, often setting up home in agricultural fields. But little is known about the behaviour of juvenile harriers once they leave the nest. This year, for the first time, the RSPB has fitted two of the chicks with satellite tags in the hope of providing the birds with better protection.

stories.title: King of Norway's health has worsened, palace says
stories.summary: Norway's King Harald V's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bloodstream bacterial infection. The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice. The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago. His son Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave. King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia. The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026. Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018. The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg Høiby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges, and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence.

stories.title: Russia’s frigate Admiral Kasatonov returns to base after long-range deployment
stories.summary: Commander of the Northern Fleet Admiral Konstantin Kabantsov received a report from the ship’s crew on the successful completion of their assigned tasks
article_sentences: MOSCOW, August 24.
The Russian Navy Northern Fleet’s frigate.
"A welcome ceremony was held in Severomorsk for the Northern Fleet frigate Admiral Kasatonov, which completed its long-range deployment and returned to base.
Commander of the Northern Fleet Admiral Konstantin Kabantsov received a report from the ship’s crew on the successful completion of their assigned tasks," the Northern Fleet noted.
The commander congratulated the Severomorsk sailors on successfully completing all their assigned tasks and returning to their home port.
He noted that "the deployment took place amid growing tensions in the international political situation, which required a high degree of professionalism, composure, and responsibility from the crew."

"For an extended period, you carried out missions of strategic deterrence in operationally critical areas of the world’s oceans, protected Russia’s maritime economic activities, ensured freedom of navigation, and contributed to strengthening international relations with countries friendly to us.
The ship’s crew demonstrated a high level of naval training, coordination, and professional skills, as well as the reliability of Russian equipment and weapons.
You have confirmed that you are capable of carrying out the most complex missions anywhere in the world’s oceans.
I am confident that you will handle future challenges facing the crew with excellent results and at the same high level," Admiral Konstantin Kabantsov emphasized at the ship’s welcome ceremony.
In keeping with tradition, the fleet commander presented the Admiral Kasatonov frigate commander with a roasted piglet, and awarded distinguished sailors with medals and certificates.
Vladimir Yevmenkov, head of the closed administrative-territorial formation of Severomorsk, also congratulated the frigate’s crew on their return home.
